a: Josiah held the Passover in Jerusalem
t: Where 1 Esdras begins, and how its verses are numbered
p: The book opens in the middle of the story told in 2 Chronicles 35, with Josiah's great Passover.
b:
1 Esdras starts with no introduction: its first word is "And." Its chapter 1 runs beside 2 Chronicles 35:1–36:21, and chapter 2 beside Ezra 1 and Ezra 4:7–24. Whether it was cut from a longer work or began here on purpose, the text does not say; the book's opening pages give the views.

Verse numbers: this site numbers 1 Esdras as Swete's Greek edition does, with 55 verses in chapter 1 and 25 in chapter 2. The KJV Apocrypha splits some verses, so it has 58 and 30. From 1:11 on, the KJV number is one higher (this site's 1:10 holds KJV 1:10–11); from 1:17, two higher (1:16 holds KJV 1:17–18); from 1:50, three higher (1:49 holds KJV 1:51–52). In chapter 2 the KJV number is one higher from 2:7 to 2:17 (2:6 holds KJV 2:6–7), and more after that: 2:15–25 here is KJV 2:16–30.

The book's names differ too. Orthodox Bibles call it 1 Ezra (The Orthodox Study Bible) or, in Slavonic and Russian, 2 Ezra, where the Russian Orthodox Theological Encyclopedia lists "2 and 3 Ezra" among the non-canonical books of the Slavonic-Russian Bible.

a: for his Lord
p: The Greek has kyrios, 'Lord,' for God. The Plain writes 'the LORD' only where the Hebrew book it retells has the name YHWH.
b: Greek has no form of God's personal name: the Septuagint writes kyrios, "Lord," for the Hebrew YHWH. Because 1 Esdras retells Chronicles and Ezra, this Plain writes "the LORD" in capitals where the Greek has kyrios and the Hebrew verse it retells has YHWH (so the two books read alike), and "the Lord" where the Hebrew has "God," where there is no Hebrew parallel (1:21–22), or where the Greek makes the word a title ("the Lord of Israel," 2:3). Here the Greek says "his Lord," a possessive the name cannot take; 2 Chronicles 35:1 has "for the LORD."
orig: τῷ κυρίῳ αὐτοῦ (tō kyriō autou), 'for his Lord'

a: dressed in their robes
p: Where Chronicles says Josiah 'strengthened' the priests, the Greek of 1 Esdras says they were robed.
b: The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 35:2 says Josiah "strengthened them" (vaychazzeqem), and the Greek of Chronicles agrees (katischysen). 1 Esdras instead pictures the priests "robed" in the temple, ready in their vestments. It also sets them out by ephēmeriai, the day-by-day shifts of priestly service (the word in Luke 1:5, 8 for Zechariah's division), where the Hebrew has their "posts."
orig: ἐστολισμένους (estolismenous), 'robed'

a: Israel's temple servants
p: Chronicles calls the Levites the men 'who taught all Israel.' 1 Esdras calls them hierodouloi, 'temple servants.'
b: The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 35:3 calls the Levites hammevinim, "those who taught" all Israel; the Greek of Chronicles has "the able men in all Israel." 1 Esdras has hierodouloi, literally "sacred slaves," a Greek word for the servants of a temple. Later the book uses the same word for the lower class of temple servants in the list of returning families (5:29, where Ezra 2:43 has "the temple servants"). Here it is an honor title for the Levites, not a rank: the Levites of 1:3 are not the lower temple servants of 5:29, though the Plain uses the same English for the same Greek word.
orig: ἱεροδούλοις τοῦ Ἰσραήλ (hierodoulois tou Israēl)

a: when the holy ark of the LORD was placed
t: The last time the ark appears
p: The last time the histories name the ark, unless 'the LORD's chests' of 1:51 mean it.
b: Chronicles has Josiah tell the Levites to set the ark in the temple, which implies it had been moved. 1 Esdras turns the order into the occasion for the Levites to make themselves holy. After this the histories do not name the ark again, unless "the LORD's chests" of 1:51 are meant to include it. Jeremiah foresees a day when "people will not say any more, 'The ark of the covenant of the LORD'" (Jeremiah 3:16). 2 Maccabees tells that Jeremiah "carried the tent, the ark and the altar of incense" into "a room like a cave" on the mountain Moses had climbed (2 Maccabees 2:4–5). For "the LORD's chests" carried to Babylon, see 1:51 and the variant there.

a: You will not have to carry it on your shoulders
p: In the wilderness the Levites carried the ark on their shoulders; with the ark at rest in the temple, that work was over.
b: The law gave the Kohathite Levites the carrying of the holy things (Numbers 4:15), and David had already declared, "there is no more carrying of the tabernacle" (1 Chronicles 23:26). Josiah's words, as both Chronicles and 1 Esdras give them, free the Levites for a new work: serving God and the people, and here slaughtering the Passover for them (1:6).

a: as befits the greatness of Solomon his son
p: The Hebrew says the Levites' order follows what David and Solomon 'wrote.' 1 Esdras has Solomon's 'majesty.'
b: In 2 Chronicles 35:4 the Levites are to arrange themselves "as David king of Israel wrote and as his son Solomon wrote": the Hebrew repeats the idea of writing (kikhtav, uvmikhtav). 1 Esdras keeps "the writing of David" but has megaleiotēs, "majesty, greatness," for Solomon. The sense becomes: in a way worthy of the splendor of Solomon's temple.
orig: κατὰ τὴν μεγαλειότητα Σαλωμὼν (kata tēn megaleiotēta Salōmōn)

a: a gift he had promised to the people, the priests and the Levites
p: In Chronicles the people, priests and Levites receive the officials' freewill gift. 1 Esdras makes them receivers of the king's own gift.
b: 2 Chronicles 35:7–8 has two gifts: Josiah's thirty thousand animals "from the king's property," and then "His officials set aside a freewill gift for the people, the priests and the Levites." 1 Esdras runs the two together: the king's gift was given "by promise" (kat' epangelian) to the people, the priests and the Levites, and the officials' names follow in 1:8. The numbers agree with the Hebrew.
orig: κατ᾽ ἐπαγγελίαν (kat' epangelian), 'by promise'

a: Esyelus
p: Where 1 Esdras has a different name from the Hebrew book, the Plain keeps the Greek name, with the Hebrew in a note.
b: Here the Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 35:8 has Jehiel, and the Greek of Chronicles Ieiēl. Swete prints Ēsyēlos; a later hand in Vaticanus wrote hē synodos, "the assembly," and the KJV has "Syelus." The rule this Plain follows in every part of the book: where the Greek name is a spelling of the same Hebrew name, the Plain uses the familiar English form (Josiah, Hilkiah, Zechariah, Nebuchadnezzar, Zedekiah). Where 1 Esdras has a different name, or turns a title into a name, the Plain keeps the Greek form (Esyelus, Sabias, Ochiel, Eddinus, Zarius, Beeltethmus), and a note gives the Hebrew. Where the Greek gives a known Bible name to a different man (Jeconiah in 1:9 and 1:32, Jehoiakim in 1:41), the Plain keeps the name and a note says who is meant. The book is not corrected to the Hebrew.
orig: Ἠσύηλος (Ēsyēlos)

a: Jeconiah
p: Not the king: this Jeconiah is a Levite leader, Konaniah in 2 Chronicles 35:9.
b: The Greek Iechonias here names a leader of the Levites, the man 2 Chronicles 35:9 calls Konaniah (Greek of Chronicles Chōnenias). The same Greek name stands in 1:32 for Josiah's son Jehoahaz, and elsewhere in the Bible Jeconiah is King Jehoiachin ("Jeconiah his son," 1 Chronicles 3:16). So one name stands for three different men: two in this chapter, and the king elsewhere. See the note on the names at 1:8.
orig: Ἰεχονίας (Iechonias)

a: commanders of thousands
p: The givers to the Levites are 'leaders of the Levites' in Chronicles, 'commanders of thousands' here, and four of the six names differ.
b: 2 Chronicles 35:9 names Konaniah, Shemaiah, Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel and Jozabad, "the leaders of the Levites." 1 Esdras has Jeconiah, Shemaiah, Nethanel "his brother," Sabias, Ochiel and Joram, and calls them chiliarchoi, "commanders of thousands," a military title. The calves are seven hundred, where the Hebrew and the Greek of Chronicles have five hundred. The number of sheep is in the variant.
orig: χιλίαρχοι (chiliarchoi)

a: They did the same in the morning
p: The Hebrew ends 'And so with the cattle.' Both Greek books have 'morning': the same Hebrew letters can be read either way.
b: 2 Chronicles 35:12 ends vekhen labbaqar, "and so with the cattle" (baqar). Written without vowels, the same letters can be read labboqer, "in the morning" (boqer). The Greek of Chronicles has "and so for the morning," and 1 Esdras "and so the morning." Both translators read the second way. The Hebrew reading fits the context better, since 35:7–9 just listed the cattle given for the feast.
orig: καὶ οὕτω τὸ πρωινόν (kai houtō to prōinon)

a: holding the unleavened bread
p: The blood and the skinning of 2 Chronicles 35:11 are missing; 1 Esdras pictures the priests and Levites holding the unleavened bread.
b: In 2 Chronicles 35:11 the priests splash the blood and the Levites skin the animals. 1 Esdras has nothing of this. Instead, the priests and Levites stand in order "having the unleavened bread" (echontes ta azyma), a detail found in neither the Hebrew nor the Greek of Chronicles. The scene becomes a procession more than a slaughter.
orig: ἔχοντες τὰ ἄζυμα (echontes ta azyma)

a: They roasted the Passover in the fire
p: Exodus says the Passover is roasted, not boiled; Deuteronomy says 'cook it.' 1 Esdras, like the Greek of Chronicles, says 'roasted.'
b: Exodus 12:9 commands: "Do not eat any of it raw, or boiled at all in water, but roasted over fire." Deuteronomy 16:7 says "Cook it," using bashal, the usual word for boiling. 2 Chronicles 35:13 brings the two together: the Hebrew says the Passover was "cooked" (bashal) "in the fire," while the other holy offerings were boiled in pots. 1 Esdras, with the Greek of Chronicles, uses the plain word for roasting (optaō), so the reader sees at once that Exodus was kept.
orig: ὤπτησαν τὸ πάσχα ἐν πυρὶ (ōptēsan to pascha en pyri)

a: with a sweet smell
t: Pans that became a sweet smell (Claude's theory)
p: Claude's theory: the Hebrew 'pans' was read as the verb 'succeed', and from there came the Greek 'sweet smell.'
b: The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 35:13 lists "pots, kettles and pans," the last word being tsallachot. Where it stands, the Greek of Chronicles has kai euodōthē, "and it went well," as if from the verb tsalach, "succeed," written with the same letters. 1 Esdras has met' euōdias, "with a sweet smell." Claude's theory, for which I know of no published support: the two Greek words sound almost alike (euodia, "success," and euōdia, "fragrance"), and 1 Esdras, or the copy behind it, took the success for the fragrance of a sacrifice (Leviticus 1:9).

a: the king's men
t: Heman and Jeduthun, Zechariah and Eddinus
p: Chronicles names Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun 'the king's visionary.' 1 Esdras has Asaph, Zechariah and Eddinus, 'those from the king.'
b: In 2 Chronicles 35:15 the singers stand "by the command of David, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun the king's visionary" (chozeh hammelekh). 1 Esdras has Zechariah where the Hebrew has Heman, Eddinus for Jeduthun, and "those from the king" (hoi para tou basileōs) for the visionary, so the three become royal appointees rather than the founders of the guilds of singers. The book calls the singers hieropsaltai, "temple harpists," its word for them throughout (5:27).
orig: οἱ παρὰ τοῦ βασιλέως (hoi para tou basileōs), 'the ones from the king'

a: since the days of Samuel the prophet
t: Since Samuel, or since the judges?
p: Kings says no such Passover had been held since the judges; Chronicles and 1 Esdras say since Samuel, the last judge.
b: 2 Kings 23:22 says, "No Passover like this one had been held since the time of the judges who led Israel." 2 Chronicles 35:18 and 1 Esdras name Samuel, the last of the judges and a prophet, and so reach past even Hezekiah's great Passover (2 Chronicles 30:26). 1 Esdras makes the same comparison as Chronicles, in slightly different Greek ("from the times of Samuel," where the Greek of Chronicles has "from the days of Samuel").

a: the Jews
p: 1 Esdras says 'the Jews' (Ioudaioi) where Chronicles says 'all Judah,' and 'Judea' for the land.
b: Where 2 Chronicles 35:18 has "all Judah," 1 Esdras has hoi Ioudaioi, "the Jews," the name used in the Persian and Greek periods (Ezra 4:12). It calls the land Ioudaia, "Judea" (1:24, 1:30, 1:31, 1:35, 1:37, 1:44; 2:4), the Greek name of the time, though it keeps Iouda, "Judah," in old phrases such as "the scroll of the kings of Israel and Judah" (1:31) and "the tribes of Judah and Benjamin" (2:7). The Plain follows the Greek in each place.
orig: οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι (hoi Ioudaioi)

a: It was in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign
t: The year the law was found
p: The eighteenth year was also the year the scroll of the law was found in the temple.
b: 2 Kings tells that "In King Josiah's eighteenth year" the king sent Shaphan to the temple, where the law scroll was found (2 Kings 22:3–8), and puts the Passover in the same year (2 Kings 23:23). 1 Esdras tells nothing of the scroll or the reform before it: the book begins with the Passover itself. Readers who know Kings or Chronicles hear in this date the whole story of the reform.

a: for they came from a heart full of godliness
t: Two verses not in the Hebrew
p: 1:21–22 have no match in the Hebrew of Chronicles. The Greek of Chronicles adds a longer passage in the same place, taken from 2 Kings 23.
b: After the date of the Passover, the Hebrew of 2 Chronicles goes straight to Neco (35:20). The Greek of Chronicles in Codex Vaticanus adds four sentences there taken from 2 Kings 23:24–27: Josiah burned the mediums and idols, no king was like him, and yet the LORD did not turn from his anger over Manasseh. 1 Esdras has its own two sentences in the same place, shorter and in different words, on the same two themes: Josiah's upright heart, and the sins that had already doomed Israel. The word for his heart is eusebeia, "godliness." The Hebrew of Chronicles has nothing here to match it; the word belongs to the vocabulary of the Greek Bible, which uses it also in Isaiah 11:2.
orig: ἐν καρδίᾳ πλήρει εὐσεβείας (en kardia plērei eusebeias)

a: The things of his time are written in the records of earlier times
p: The Greek may mean that his times are recorded in earlier histories, or that the sins were written down long before.
b: Word for word: "and the things about him have been written in the former times, about those who had sinned..." One reading: the record of Josiah's age is found in the earlier histories (Kings). Another: what was coming on Judah had been written down long before, as in the warnings of the law and the prophets. The KJV takes it the first way. Either way the sentence moves the blame from Josiah to the people of his time, who sinned "more than any nation or kingdom" (compare 2 Kings 21:9: "they did worse evil than the nations the LORD wiped out ahead of the Israelites").
orig: καὶ τὰ κατ᾽ αὐτὸν δὲ ἀναγέγραπται ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν χρόνοις

a: And the words of the Lord rose up against Israel
t: Compared with the Bible: a good king, a fixed judgment
p: Agrees with 2 Kings: Josiah was upright, yet the judgment for earlier sins stood.
b: 1 Esdras here agrees with the 66 books. 2 Kings praises Josiah above every king (2 Kings 23:25) and in the next breath says the LORD did not turn from his anger (2 Kings 23:26–27); Huldah told Josiah that the disaster would come, but not in his days (2 Kings 22:16–20). 1 Esdras puts the same tension in a single sentence, using the picture of God's words "rising up" against Israel. Chronicles leaves this out and passes straight to Josiah's death.

a: Pharaoh king of Egypt
p: The Pharaoh, unnamed here, was Neco II. In 609 BC he marched north to the Euphrates, and Josiah tried to stop him.
b: 1 Esdras never names the Pharaoh; 2 Chronicles 35:20 and 2 Kings 23:29 call him Neco. Kings says he "marched up toward the king of Assyria, to the Euphrates River," and he was going to help the Assyrian empire against Babylon. Carchemish, on the upper Euphrates, is where Nebuchadnezzar later struck down Neco's army "in the fourth year of Jehoiakim" (Jeremiah 46:2). Josephus says Neco wanted "to reign over Asia" and was going to fight the Medes and Babylonians (Antiquities 10.74).

a: It is not against you that the Lord God has sent me out
p: Chronicles says Neco's words came 'from God's mouth.' 1 Esdras gives them in the Lord's name, then moves the warning to Jeremiah.
b:
In 2 Chronicles 35:21–22 Neco says "God bade me hurry," and the narrator says Josiah "did not listen to Neco's words from God's mouth." That a pagan king spoke for God needs explaining, and three answers are on record:

He did. Taken at its word, Chronicles says so: on this view God can speak through a foreign king, as through Cyrus (2:2).

He spoke of his own god. In the Talmud, Rav says Neco's "God who is with me" was the idol he carried (Taanit 22b).

God spoke through Jeremiah. 1 Esdras keeps Neco's claim, now in the name "the Lord," but says Josiah ignored "the words of Jeremiah the prophet from the mouth of the Lord" (1:26). See the note there.

a: the words of Jeremiah the prophet from the mouth of the Lord
p: The largest change in the chapter: the warning Josiah ignored becomes a prophet's word, not Pharaoh's.
b: Where 2 Chronicles 35:22 says Josiah "did not listen to Neco's words from God's mouth," 1 Esdras says he did not heed "the words of Jeremiah the prophet from the mouth of the Lord." No book of the Hebrew Bible records such a warning by Jeremiah. The Talmud reaches a similar answer by another road: Rabbi Yohanan says Josiah was punished because he did not consult Jeremiah before going to war, trusting instead the promise that "no sword will pass through your land" (Leviticus 26:6; Taanit 22b). Josephus mentions no warning at all and blames fate (Antiquities 10.76). Whether 1 Esdras found "Jeremiah" in its Hebrew copy or changed the text to protect God's word from a pagan mouth is not known.

a: He set out to fight him
p: Chronicles says Josiah disguised himself, like Ahab before his death. 1 Esdras says only that he set out to fight.
b: The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 35:22 says, "He disguised himself to fight him" (hitchappes), the same verb used of King Ahab, who also went into battle in disguise and died of an arrow in his chariot (1 Kings 22:30–35). The Greek of Chronicles has "he strengthened himself," and 1 Esdras "he undertook" (epicheirei) to fight him. The likeness to Ahab is lost in both Greek books.
orig: πολεμεῖν αὐτὸν ἐπιχειρεῖ (polemein auton epicheirei)

a: the plain of Megiddo
p: The Greek name is garbled (Metaaddous). Megiddo guarded the main pass of the coast road; Armageddon takes its name from it.
b: Codex Vaticanus spells the place Metaaddous and Alexandrinus Metaeddaous, forms that seem to have grown out of the Hebrew Megiddo; the Greek of Chronicles has "the plain of Magedon." Megiddo commanded the pass where the coast road crosses into the Jezreel Valley, so armies met there again and again. Zechariah remembers "the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo" (Zechariah 12:11), and Revelation's "Armageddon" (Revelation 16:16) is usually explained as "the mountain of Megiddo." Josephus calls the place Mendes (Antiquities 10.75).
orig: ἐν τῷ πεδίῳ Μετααδδοῦς (en tō pediō Metaaddous)

a: the officers came down against King Josiah
p: The Hebrew says 'the archers shot at King Josiah.' 1 Esdras has 'the rulers came down against' him.
b: In 2 Chronicles 35:23 "The shooters shot at King Josiah" (vayyoru hayyorim), and the Greek of Chronicles has "the archers." 1 Esdras has hoi archontes, "the rulers, officers." So the arrow is gone, and in 1:28 Josiah is "weakened" rather than "hurt." Josephus keeps the arrow: an Egyptian archer shot him (Antiquities 10.77).
orig: οἱ ἄρχοντες (hoi archontes)

a: He climbed into his second chariot
p: Kings says Neco killed Josiah at Megiddo; Chronicles and 1 Esdras say he was wounded there and died in Jerusalem.
b: 2 Kings 23:29–30 is brief: "the moment Neco saw him, he put him to death at Megiddo," and his servants carried "his dead body" home. 2 Chronicles 35:24 says his servants moved him to his second chariot and he died in Jerusalem. 1 Esdras has Josiah climb into the chariot himself and die after reaching Jerusalem: metēllaxen ton bion autou, "he exchanged his life," a Greek way of saying he died. Josephus also has him die of his wound in Jerusalem (Antiquities 10.77).

a: Jeremiah the prophet sang a lament over Josiah
p: Chronicles says Jeremiah's lament was 'written in the Laments.' Later Jews connected it with Lamentations 4:20.
b: Chronicles adds, "you will find them written in the Laments" (2 Chronicles 35:25); 1 Esdras leaves this out. Josephus says Jeremiah composed an elegy for Josiah "which is extant till this time also" (Antiquities 10.78, Whiston's translation). The Talmud says that as Josiah died he said, "The LORD is righteous, for I defied his command" (Lamentations 1:18), and that Jeremiah began his lament with "The breath of our nostrils, the LORD's anointed, was trapped in their pits" (Lamentations 4:20; Taanit 22b). Compare the mourning "in the plain of Megiddo" in Zechariah 12:11.

a: the chief men and the women
p: The Hebrew has 'male and female singers.' The Greek of Chronicles has 'rulers, men and women'; 1 Esdras 'the chief men, with women.'
b: In 2 Chronicles 35:25 the mourners are hassharim vehassharot, "the male singers and the female singers," professional mourners. The Greek of Chronicles has hoi archontes kai hai archousai, "the rulers and the women rulers," reading the same consonants (שרים) as sarim, "princes," instead of sharim, "singers": in the unpointed text the two words are identical, and only the dot on the letter shin/sin tells them apart. 1 Esdras has hoi prokathēmenoi syn gynaixin, "those who preside, with women." It thus agrees with the Greek of Chronicles in making the mourners leading men.
orig: οἱ προκαθήμενοι σὺν γυναιξὶν (hoi prokathēmenoi syn gynaixin)

a: his glory, and his understanding in the LORD's law
p: Where Chronicles praises Josiah's 'acts of loyal love,' 1 Esdras praises his glory and his understanding of the law.
b: 2 Chronicles 35:26 speaks of Josiah's chasadav, "his acts of loyal love in keeping with what is written in the LORD's law." 1 Esdras has "his glory and his understanding in the law of the Lord," a portrait of a wise and learned king. It also names two books where Chronicles has one: "the scroll of the histories about Judea's kings" and "the scroll of the kings of Israel and Judah." Whether these are two works or one named twice is not clear.
orig: τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ καὶ τῆς συνέσεως αὐτοῦ (tēs doxēs autou kai tēs syneseōs autou)

a: Jehoiakim, his brother,
p: Josiah's son, the king of 2 Kings 23:34–24:6. Kings and Chronicles say Pharaoh renamed him; 1 Esdras does not.
b: 2 Kings 23:34 says Neco "put Eliakim son of Josiah on the throne... and turned his name into Jehoiakim," a sign that he was Egypt's vassal; 2 Chronicles 36:4 says the same. 1 Esdras leaves out the old name and the renaming. It also leaves out the length of his reign (eleven years, 2 Chronicles 36:5) in 1:37. The Jehoiakim of 1:41 is a different man, his son, whom the Hebrew calls Jehoiachin.
orig: Ἰωακεὶμ τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ (Iōakeim ton adelphon autou)

a: Jehoiakim bound the nobles
p: The Greek name does not change form, so it may be the subject or the object. The KJV read 'he bound Joacim and the nobles.'
b: The Greek reads kai edēsen Iōakeim tous megistanas. Greek names taken over from Hebrew often do not change their endings, so Iōakeim could be either the one who bound or the one bound. Read as subject, the new king arrests the nobles who had made his brother king. Read as object (with "and" supplied), Pharaoh binds Jehoiakim and the nobles; the KJV has "he bound Joacim and the nobles." The Plain takes the plainer grammar but keeps the Greek order so that both readings stay open.
orig: καὶ ἔδησεν Ἰωακεὶμ τοὺς μεγιστᾶνας (kai edēsen Iōakeim tous megistanas)

a: brought up out of Egypt
t: To Egypt or out of Egypt?
p: In the Hebrew, Neco takes the deposed king to Egypt. The Greek of 1 Esdras says 'brought up out of Egypt.'
b: 2 Chronicles 36:4 says, "Joahaz his brother, Neco took away and brought to Egypt," and 2 Kings 23:34 adds that he died there. The Greek of 1 Esdras has anēgagen ex Aigyptou, "he led up out of Egypt," and calls the brother Zarius. Swete's notes show no manuscript reading "to Egypt," so the Plain keeps what the Greek says. As it stands, the verse does not fit the history the other books tell.
orig: ἀνήγαγεν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου (anēgagen ex Aigyptou)

a: He bound him in bronze fetters and took him away to Babylon
p: Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim 'to take him to Babylon.' 1 Esdras says he did take him. Kings says he died at home.
b: 2 Chronicles 36:6 says Nebuchadnezzar "bound him in bronze fetters to take him to Babylon," without saying he went. 2 Kings 24:6 says "Jehoiakim lay down with his ancestors," the usual phrase for a death at home, and Jeremiah foretold that he would be "buried the way a donkey is buried" outside Jerusalem (Jeremiah 22:19). Daniel 1:2 says "The Lord handed Jehoiakim king of Judah over to him." 1 Esdras settles the question in one direction: he was led away to Babylon. The Greek of Chronicles in Vaticanus adds several sentences on his reign after 36:5.

a: he put them in his temple in Babylon
p: The temple vessels go to Babylon here and in 1:43 and 1:51, and they come home in 2:9–14.
b: The holy vessels are a thread through the whole book: taken in three stages (1:39; 1:43; 1:51), handed back by Cyrus (2:9–14), and brought into the rebuilt temple (6:17–18). Daniel tells that Nebuchadnezzar put them in "the treasury of that god's house" (Daniel 1:2), and that Belshazzar drank from them at his feast (Daniel 5:2–4). For the exiles, their return showed that the new temple was the same house as the old.

a: his son Jehoiakim
t: Father and son with one name
p: The Greek gives the son the same name as his father, Ioakeim. The Hebrew calls him Jehoiachin; Greek Chronicles calls him Jeconiah.
b: In Hebrew the two kings' names differ by two letters: Jehoiakim (Yehoyaqim) and his son Jehoiachin (Yehoyakhin), also called Jeconiah. 1 Esdras writes both as Iōakeim, and the KJV, "Joacim his son," does the same. The Greek of Chronicles has Iechonias, Jeconiah. 1 Esdras uses that name instead for Jehoahaz in 1:32 (in Vaticanus). So the names of Josiah's line are shuffled in this book: Jeconiah stands for Jehoahaz, and Jehoiakim for Jehoiachin. The Plain keeps the Greek names, and the notes say who is meant.
orig: Ἰωακεὶμ ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ (Iōakeim ho huios autou)

a: A year later
t: At the turn of the year
p: The Hebrew says 'at the turn of the year,' the spring, when kings went to war. 1 Esdras has 'after a year.'
b: 2 Chronicles 36:10 says litshuvat hashshanah, "at the turn of the year," the season when kings marched out (compare 2 Samuel 11:1). 1 Esdras has met' eniauton, "after a year," which makes the young king reign a year, though 1:42 says three months and ten days. 2 Kings 24:10–17 tells this first capture of Jerusalem (597 BC) at length.
orig: μετ᾽ ἐνιαυτὸν (met' eniauton)

a: He set up Zedekiah as king of Judea and Jerusalem
p: Chronicles calls Zedekiah Jehoiachin's 'brother,' Kings his 'uncle,' Greek Chronicles 'his father's brother.' 1 Esdras gives no relation.
b: The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 36:10 calls Zedekiah "his brother" (achiv); 2 Kings 24:17 says Mattaniah was "his uncle" (dodo) and renamed him Zedekiah; the Greek of Chronicles has "his father's brother." 1 Esdras says only that Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah king, which avoids the conflict. Jeremiah 37:1 calls Zedekiah "son of Josiah," which agrees with Kings.
orig: ἀνέδειξε Σεδεκίαν βασιλέα (anedeixe Sedekian basilea)

a: put him under oath by the name of the Lord
p: Zedekiah swore loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar in God's name and broke it. Ezekiel treats the broken oath as a sin against God himself.
b: Ezekiel tells the same event as a riddle: the king of Babylon "took one of the royal family and made a covenant with him. He made him swear an oath" (Ezekiel 17:13), and because Zedekiah broke it, God says, "the oath he despised is my oath" (Ezekiel 17:19). 1 Esdras, like Chronicles, says the oath was sworn "by the name of the Lord" and calls the rebellion a false oath (ephiorkēsas).

a: for his tent
p: The Greek calls God's dwelling his skēnōma, 'tent,' the word that recalls the tabernacle.
b: Where 2 Chronicles 36:15 says God "felt pity for his people and for the place where he lived" (me'ono, "his dwelling"), 1 Esdras has skēnōma, "tent, dwelling." The Greek Old Testament often uses words of this family for the tabernacle, so the temple is pictured as God's tent among his people. In 2:5 Cyrus calls God "the Lord who has made his dwelling (kataskēnōsas) in Jerusalem," with the same root.
orig: τοῦ σκηνώματος αὐτοῦ (tou skēnōmatos autou)

a: the kings of the Chaldeans
p: Chronicles says God raised up 'the king of the Chaldeans.' 1 Esdras has the plural.
b: 2 Chronicles 36:17 has one king, Nebuchadnezzar. 1 Esdras has "the kings of the Chaldeans," and goes on with plural verbs ("They killed," 1:50). The Chaldeans were a people of the far south of Mesopotamia; the line of kings that ruled Babylon at the height of its power, from Nabopolassar to its fall in 539 BC, is called the Chaldean dynasty, so the name stands for Babylon.
orig: τοὺς βασιλεῖς τῶν Χαλδαίων (tous basileis tōn Chaldaiōn)

a: until seventy years are filled up
p: Chronicles and 1 Esdras join Jeremiah's seventy years to the law's warning that the land would rest while Israel was in exile.
b: Two texts are joined here. Leviticus 26:34 warns: "Then the land will make up for its Sabbaths, all the days it lies desolate while you are in your enemies' land." Jeremiah gives the length: "these nations will serve the king of Babylon seventy years" (Jeremiah 25:11; compare Jeremiah 29:10). The idea that the seventy years repaid the Sabbath years Israel had not kept is drawn out of the two together. Daniel later meditates on the same number (Daniel 9:2). 1 Esdras puts the land's rest in the future tense: "it will keep Sabbath."

a: In the first year that Cyrus reigned over the Persians
t: Where Chronicles ends and Ezra begins
p: 2:1–5 is the decree that both ends 2 Chronicles (36:22–23) and opens Ezra (1:1–3). In 1 Esdras it simply follows on.
b: In the Hebrew Bible, Cyrus's decree appears twice: at the very end of 2 Chronicles (cut off at "and let him go up") and at the start of Ezra. 1 Esdras runs from Josiah's Passover through the fall of Jerusalem into the decree with no break, as if Chronicles and Ezra were one continuous history. Whether that means Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah once formed one work is a question taken up on the book's opening pages. Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC.

a: has appointed me king of the whole inhabited world
p: Ezra has 'All the kingdoms of the earth the LORD... has given me.' 1 Esdras: God made him king of the oikoumenē.
b: Ezra 1:2 reads, "All the kingdoms of the earth the LORD, the God of the heavens, has given me." 1 Esdras has Cyrus say that "the Lord of Israel, the Lord Most High" made him king of the oikoumenē, the whole inhabited world, the word Luke uses of Augustus's census ("the whole inhabited world was to be registered," Luke 2:1). Josephus, who follows 1 Esdras here, has Cyrus say God "hath appointed me to be king of the habitable earth" (Antiquities 11.3, Whiston), and adds that Cyrus read his own name in Isaiah (11.5; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1).
orig: Ἐμὲ ἀνέδειξεν βασιλέα τῆς οἰκουμένης (Eme anedeixen basilea tēs oikoumenēs)

a: the Lord Most High
p: For Ezra's 'the God of the heavens,' 1 Esdras has 'the Lord Most High,' the Septuagint's title for God as Elyon.
b: Ezra's title for God in Persian letters is "the God of the heavens" (Ezra 1:2; 5:11–12). 1 Esdras gives Cyrus two titles: "the Lord of Israel" and Kyrios ho hypsistos, "the Lord Most High." Hypsistos, "highest," is the Septuagint's word for Elyon (Genesis 14:18–20), and in the Bible outsiders, too, speak of "the Most High God": Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:2) and the slave girl at Philippi (Acts 16:17).
orig: Κύριος ὁ ὕψιστος (Kyrios ho hypsistos)

a: with horses and livestock
p: 1 Esdras adds horses to the gifts (2:6, 2:8) and calls the freewill offerings 'vows.'
b: Ezra 1:4 and 1:6 list silver, gold, goods and livestock, and a "freewill offering." 1 Esdras adds horses both times, and calls the gifts things given "by vow" (kat' euchas), promises made to God. Horses were costly gifts for a long road: the list of returning families counts 736 horses (Ezra 2:66).
orig: μεθ᾽ ἵππων καὶ κτηνῶν (meth' hippōn kai ktēnōn)

a: his idol temple
p: Ezra says 'his gods' house.' 1 Esdras uses eidōlion, 'idol temple,' the word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 8:10.
b: Ezra 1:7 says Nebuchadnezzar put the vessels "in his gods' house." 1 Esdras uses eidōlion, a scornful Jewish Greek word for a pagan temple, built on eidōlon, "idol." Paul uses a form of the same word: "sitting at a meal in an idol's temple" (1 Corinthians 8:10). 1:39 had called the same building "his temple."
orig: ἐν τῷ εἰδωλίῳ αὐτοῦ (en tō eidōliō autou)

a: the leader of Judea
p: The man Ezra 1:8 calls Sheshbazzar is Sanassar here and Samanassar in 2:14; Josephus and the KJV have Sanabassar.
b: Ezra 1:8 names "Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah" (hannasi). Codex Vaticanus spells him Sanassaros here and Samanassaros in 2:14; a corrector of Alexandrinus wrote Sanabassaros here (over an erasure), Alexandrinus has Samabassaros in 2:14, and the KJV and Josephus (Antiquities 11.11) have "Sanabassar." The Plain keeps Vaticanus's two forms so the reader sees the text; both mean the same man. His title here is prostatēs, "leader, protector." Who he was, and whether he is Zerubbabel under another name, is discussed on the topic page; in 1 Esdras, Zerubbabel's own return comes later (5:1–8).
orig: Σανασσάρῳ προστάτῃ τῆς Ἰουδαίας (Sanassarō prostatē tēs Ioudaias)

a: This was their count
p: Ezra's list of vessels comes to 2,499, though its total says 5,400. The list in 1 Esdras adds up exactly to its total of 5,469.
b: Ezra 1:9–11 lists 30 + 1,000 + 29 + 30 + 410 + 1,000 = 2,499 vessels, yet gives the total as 5,400. 1 Esdras lists 1,000 + 1,000 + 29 + 30 + 2,410 + 1,000 = 5,469, and its total (2:13) is exactly that. Either 1 Esdras kept a better copy of the list, or someone made the numbers agree. The kinds of vessels differ too: Ezra's "gold basins" are "gold cups for drink offerings," and its "knives" are "censers." Josephus gives yet other numbers, including 2,400 silver bowls (Antiquities 11.15).

a: 2,410 silver bowls
p: Claude's theory: Ezra's 'of a second kind' (mishnim) was read as 'two thousand.'
b: Ezra 1:10 has "410 silver bowls of a second kind," where "of a second kind" is the rare Hebrew mishnim. Vaticanus writes the number with Greek letter numerals, BY' (2,400), plus the word "ten"; Alexandrinus spells out "two thousand four hundred" before the "ten." Claude's theory, for which I know of no published support: a translator took mishnim, "second," as a form of "two" and read it as "two thousand"; with 410 that makes 2,410, and the total comes out as 5,469. The step from "second" to "two thousand" is a long one, and Josephus's figure of 2,400 silver bowls (Antiquities 11.15) shows that a number of 2,400 was known in its own right, so the theory is weak. If it holds, the Greek total was worked out from the list, not the list from the total.

a: In the time of Artaxerxes king of the Persians
p: 1 Esdras puts Artaxerxes' letter before the temple was built under Darius, though Artaxerxes reigned after Darius.
b: In Ezra, chapter 4 jumps forward: after the opposition under Cyrus and Darius (Ezra 4:1–5), it gives later complaints under Ahasuerus (Xerxes) and Artaxerxes about the city walls (Ezra 4:6–23), then returns to the temple under Darius (4:24). 1 Esdras places the Artaxerxes letter right after Cyrus, so the order reads: Cyrus, Artaxerxes, Darius. The Persian kings ran Cyrus, Cambyses, Darius I, Xerxes, Artaxerxes I. Josephus saw the problem and named the king Cambyses, son of Cyrus (Antiquities 11.21). The text does not say whether the writer of 1 Esdras read Ezra 4 as one straight sequence or kept an older order of the material; see the chapter page.

a: Beeltethmus
t: A title that became a name
p: Beeltethmus is the Aramaic title of Ezra 4:8, be'el te'em, 'master of the decree,' read as a man's name.
b: Ezra 4:8 introduces "Rehum the chief official" (Aramaic be'el te'em, literally "lord of decree"). 1 Esdras turns the title into a person, Beeltethmos, and lists him beside Rathymus, who gets a different title, "the recorder" (2:16). The other names are Greek forms of Ezra's: Belemus for Bishlam (which the Greek of Ezra 4:7 takes as "in peace"), Mithridates for Mithredath (Vaticanus spells him Mithridatēs in 2:10 and Mithradatēs here, and Swete's notes show the copies varying between the two; the Plain uses one English form for the one man), Tabellius for Tabeel, Rathymus for Rehum, Samellius for Shimshai. Josephus has the same three, Rathumus, Beeltethmus and Semellius (Antiquities 11.22, 26), which shows he was reading 1 Esdras.
orig: Βεέλτεθμος (Beeltethmos); Aramaic בְּעֵל טְעֵם

a: Rathymus the recorder
p: Rathymus is 'the one who writes what happens,' a court reporter. Ezra calls Rehum the 'chief official.'
b: The Greek ho ta prospiptonta, spelled out in 2:21 as "the one writing the things that befall," is an official who records events and reports them to the king. The KJV has "the storywriter," Josephus "the historiographer" (Antiquities 11.22). Ezra gives Rehum the title "chief official," which 1 Esdras has turned into the name Beeltethmus (2:15).
orig: Ῥάθυμος ὁ τὰ προσπίπτοντα (Rhathymos ho ta prospiptonta)

a: laying the foundation of a temple
t: Compared with the Bible: the temple in the letter
p: In Ezra the complaint is about the city and its walls. 1 Esdras adds the temple, and so ties this letter to the stopping of the temple work.
b: Ezra's letter says only, "They are building the rebellious and evil city. They have finished the walls and are repairing the foundations" (Ezra 4:12). It says nothing of a temple, and the king's reply stops the city, not the temple (Ezra 4:21). 1 Esdras adds the temple three times: here, in 2:18 ("the temple work is moving ahead") and in 2:25 ("Work on the temple in Jerusalem stopped"). It also adds "marketplaces." The change makes the story hang together: the letter becomes the reason the temple stood half built until Darius. Here 1 Esdras goes beyond Ezra and, on the order of events, differs from it (see 2:15).

a: set up sieges in it
p: Ezra speaks of revolt made in the city. 1 Esdras speaks of sieges or blockades organized there.
b: Ezra 4:15 has the Aramaic eshtaddur, "revolt, rebellion." 1 Esdras has poliorkias synestamenoi, "having organized sieges," picturing Jerusalem as a base for wars against its neighbors, which fits its next charge, that the city's kings ruled the whole region (2:23).
orig: πολιορκίας συνεσταμένοι (poliorkias synestamenoi)

a: Coele-Syria and Phoenicia
t: Coele-Syria: the name of the Greek age
p: Ezra says 'Beyond the River,' the Persian province. 1 Esdras uses the name of the Greek age, Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.
b: Ezra 4:16 warns that the king "will have no share left in Beyond the River," the Persian name for the province west of the Euphrates. 1 Esdras has "Coele-Syria and Phoenicia," "Hollow Syria" and the coast. That was the name of the region under the Greek kings who ruled after Alexander: in 217 BC Antiochus III made an officer governor "of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia," and 1 and 2 Maccabees use the name (1 Maccabees 10:69; 2 Maccabees 3:5). The Greek gives the region the name its readers knew; Josephus repeats the phrase (Antiquities 11.25).

a: nothing more is done against this order
p: Ezra's Artaxerxes stops the building 'until I give the order.' 1 Esdras leaves out the opening for a later decree.
b: Ezra 4:21 reads, "So now give an order to stop these men, so that this city is not built until I give the order." Those last words leave room for a change of mind, and the same Artaxerxes later sends Nehemiah to rebuild the walls (Nehemiah 2:1–8). 1 Esdras has no such clause: the king forbids that anything be done "beside these things." 1 Esdras does not tell Nehemiah's story.
orig: ὅπως μηθὲν παρὰ ταῦτα γένηται (hopōs mēthen para tauta genētai)

a: with horsemen and a crowd drawn up for battle
p: Ezra says the officials stopped the Jews 'with force and might.' 1 Esdras gives them cavalry and a battle line.
b: Ezra 4:23 says the officials "made them stop with force and might." 1 Esdras pictures it: they hurry to Jerusalem "with horse and a crowd in battle array" (meth' hippou kai ochlou parataxeōs). Josephus says they "brought a great company with them" (Antiquities 11.29, Whiston's translation).
orig: μεθ᾽ ἵππου καὶ ὄχλου παρατάξεως (meth' hippou kai ochlou parataxeōs)

a: until the second year of the reign of Darius king of the Persians
p: Darius I's second year was 520 BC, when Haggai and Zechariah began to preach. In 1 Esdras the next chapter opens at Darius's court.
b: The date matches Ezra 4:24 and Haggai 1:1 ("in the second year of King Darius"), which is 520 BC. In Ezra, the next chapter brings Haggai and Zechariah. In 1 Esdras, chapter 3 begins instead with Darius's great feast and the contest of his three guards, which explains how Zerubbabel won leave to build. Josephus, having named the king Cambyses, says the work stopped "till the second year of the reign of Darius, for nine years more" (Antiquities 11.30).
